description: Frontal, transverse and sagittal planes and frontal, transverse and longitudinal axes in sporting actions.
content_html:
Imagining the Body in Three Dimensions

When a gymnast performs a forward roll, a discus thrower spins in a full circle, or a dancer executes a cartwheel, their body is moving through space in a precise, describable way. Movement analysts use a system of planes and axes to describe exactly which direction that movement occurs and around which line the body rotates. Mastering this system is essential for analysing sport performance.

Imagine the body standing upright in the anatomical position — feet together, palms facing forwards. Now picture three flat sheets of glass slicing through the body, each at right angles to the others. These are the three planes of movement. For every plane there is a matching axis: a rod passing through the body at right angles to that plane, forming the pivot point for rotation in that plane.

Key Fact

OCR’s three planes and their matching axes: sagittal plane → transverse axis; frontal plane → frontal axis; transverse plane → longitudinal axis. Note that OCR names the axis for the frontal plane as the frontal axis (not the sagittal axis used by some other boards). Learn the OCR terms precisely.

The Sagittal Plane and Transverse Axis

The sagittal plane runs from front to back, dividing the body into a left half and a right half. Movement in this plane involves the body moving forwards or backwards. The matching axis is the transverse axis, which runs from side to side like a rod passing through both hips.

Classic sporting actions in the sagittal plane include a forward somersault (gymnastics or trampolining) and a forward roll. In both cases the body rotates in a forwards direction around the transverse axis. Running also takes place primarily in the sagittal plane, as the arms and legs swing forwards and backwards. A back somersault is also in the sagittal plane, but the rotation is in the opposite direction around the same transverse axis.

A common misconception is that any large movement must involve multiple planes. In running, the limbs swing forward and backward — that is purely sagittal-plane motion. A cartwheel, however, takes the body to the side rather than forward: the legs move apart and the body tips sideways, rotating around the frontal axis in the frontal plane. The key question is always: “Which direction does the body travel, and around which axis does it rotate?” Always answer both before identifying the plane and axis.

The Frontal Plane and Frontal Axis

The frontal plane runs from side to side, dividing the body into a front half and a back half. Movements in this plane take the body out to the side or bring it back in. The matching axis is the frontal axis, which runs from front to back like a rod passing through the navel and the spine.

The cartwheel is the clearest sporting example of the frontal plane. The gymnast tips their entire body sideways over their hands, rotating around the frontal axis. Abduction and adduction movements at the shoulder and hip also occur in the frontal plane — for instance, a star jump sees the arms and legs moving away from and back to the midline of the body in the frontal plane around the frontal axis.

The Transverse Plane and Longitudinal Axis

The transverse plane runs horizontally, dividing the body into an upper half and a lower half. Think of it as a table top cutting through the body at waist height. Movements in this plane involve twisting or spinning. The matching axis is the longitudinal axis, which runs from the top of the head straight down through the spine to the feet.

Sporting examples of transverse-plane movement around the longitudinal axis include a 360° twist in ice skating, a discus thrower rotating in a circle before release, and a figure skater pulling in their arms to spin faster. In all of these, the performer is rotating horizontally around a vertical axis running through the middle of their body.

Key Fact

The three OCR sporting triplets: forward somersault → sagittal plane, transverse axis. Cartwheel → frontal plane, frontal axis. 360° spin / ice spin → transverse plane, longitudinal axis. Commit these to memory as a set — exam questions ask you to identify both the plane and the axis.

Applying Planes and Axes to Joint Movements

The plane-and-axis framework also maps directly onto the joint movements covered in the musculoskeletal system. Flexion and extension occur in the sagittal plane around the transverse axis. Abduction and adduction occur in the frontal plane around the frontal axis. Rotation at the shoulder or hip occurs in the transverse plane around the longitudinal axis. This connection means that when you analyse a sporting action, you can describe both the joint movement and the plane and axis in which it occurs, giving a much richer technical account.

A very important distinction: OCR names the axis associated with the frontal plane as the frontal axis. Some other boards call this the “sagittal axis.” If you have studied another board’s materials, you must use OCR’s terminology in your exam answers or risk losing marks. The three OCR axes are: transverse axis (for the sagittal plane), frontal axis (for the frontal plane), and longitudinal axis (for the transverse plane). Never write “sagittal axis” in an OCR answer — this is not a term OCR uses for axes of rotation.
exam_tip_html: Questions on planes and axes typically ask you to identify both the plane and axis for a named sporting action — always give both. A common error is naming only the plane without the axis. Remember OCR’s three triplets: forward somersault (sagittal plane, transverse axis), cartwheel (frontal plane, frontal axis), 360° spin (transverse plane, longitudinal axis). Critically, OCR uses “frontal axis” for the axis of the frontal plane — not “sagittal axis.” Writing “sagittal axis” on an OCR paper will cost marks. On ‘explain’ questions, add one sentence describing the direction of rotation: “A forward somersault occurs in the sagittal plane because the body rotates forwards and backwards around the transverse axis, which runs from side to side through the hips.” For extended-response questions, connect the plane-and-axis description to the joint action (flexion, abduction) and the muscles involved.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three planes divide the body into halves — sagittal (left/right), frontal (front/back) and transverse (upper/lower) — and each has a matching axis at right angles to it: transverse axis, frontal axis and longitudinal axis respectively.
  • The three OCR triplets to memorise: forward somersault (sagittal plane, transverse axis), cartwheel (frontal plane, frontal axis) and 360° ice spin (transverse plane, longitudinal axis).
  • OCR uses “frontal axis” (not sagittal axis) for rotations in the frontal plane. Joint movements map to planes: flexion/extension in the sagittal plane, abduction/adduction in the frontal plane, rotation in the transverse plane.

practice_questions.text: Identify the plane of movement used during a forward somersault.

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a vertical axis; 1 mark for stating it runs from the top of the head to the feet (or through the spine vertically) and that the body rotates around it during spinning or twisting actions (e.g. a 360 degree turn in ice skating).

practice_questions.text: Describe the plane and axis of movement used when a gymnast performs a cartwheel. Include the direction of movement in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the frontal plane; 1 mark for identifying the frontal axis (do NOT accept 'sagittal axis' — this is not OCR terminology); 1 mark for describing the direction of movement as side-to-side (the body tips laterally over the hands, moving away from the midline).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a discus thrower spinning in a full circle before release uses the transverse plane and longitudinal axis rather than any other plane-and-axis combination.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating the movement is a horizontal rotation or spin; 1 mark for identifying the transverse plane (which divides the body into upper and lower halves); 1 mark for identifying the longitudinal axis (which runs vertically from head to feet); 1 mark for explaining that because the thrower rotates around a vertical axis rather than forwards/backwards or side-to-side, neither the sagittal nor frontal planes apply.

practice_questions.text: State two joint movements that occur in the sagittal plane, and give a sporting example of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct movement with a valid sporting example. Accept: flexion (e.g. bending the knee during a squat / bringing the thigh forward in running); extension (e.g. straightening the knee during a kick / the follow-through of a throw). Both answers must name the movement and give a sporting context. Two near-identical examples of the same movement (e.g. two examples of flexion) score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: A sports science student is asked to analyse the movement of a figure skater performing a spin followed by a jump that involves a forward somersault rotation. Analyse how the planes and axes of movement change between the spin and the somersault.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly identifies the transverse plane and longitudinal axis for the spin, with explanation that the body rotates horizontally around a vertical axis; clearly identifies the sagittal plane and transverse axis for the forward somersault, with explanation that the body rotates forward around a side-to-side axis; analyses what changes between the two movements (rotation shifts from vertical/longitudinal axis during the spin to horizontal/transverse axis during the somersault); links both to how coaching cues could reinforce the correct axis (e.g. for the spin the coach would cue the athlete to keep their longitudinal axis straight; for the somersault they would cue tucking to increase rotation speed around the transverse axis). Sustained sporting application throughout.

Secure: Correctly identifies both plane-axis pairs; some explanation of direction of rotation; limited or inconsistent application to coaching.

Developing: One plane-axis pair correctly identified; basic description of direction of movement; little or no coaching application.

Emerging: One relevant term used (plane or axis) with minimal explanation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which axis does the body rotate around during a forward roll?
A cartwheel takes place in which plane of movement?
A 360 degree spin in ice skating occurs in the _____ plane around the longitudinal axis.
In OCR, the axis matching the frontal plane is called the _____ axis.
Match each sporting action to its correct plane of movement:

flashcard_questions.a: An imaginary vertical plane dividing the body into left and right halves; movements in this plane are forward or backward.
An imaginary vertical plane dividing the body into front and back halves; movements in this plane are side-to-side.
An imaginary horizontal plane dividing the body into upper and lower halves; movements in this plane involve twisting or spinning.

flashcard_questions.q: Which axis matches the sagittal plane in OCR?
flashcard_questions.a: Transverse axis — runs side to side through the hips.

flashcard_questions.q: Which axis matches the frontal plane in OCR?
flashcard_questions.a: Frontal axis — runs front to back through the body. Note: OCR does NOT use the term 'sagittal axis'.

flashcard_questions.q: Which axis matches the transverse plane in OCR?
flashcard_questions.a: Longitudinal axis — runs vertically from head to feet.

flashcard_questions.q: A forward somersault uses which plane and axis?
A cartwheel uses which plane and axis?
A 360 degree ice spin uses which plane and axis?
Flexion and extension at the elbow occur in which plane?
Abduction and adduction at the shoulder occur in which plane?

flashcard_questions.a: A vertical axis running from head to feet around which twisting and spinning rotations occur.

glossary_terms.definition: An imaginary flat surface that divides the body into two equal sections, used to describe the direction of movement.
An imaginary straight line around which the body or a body part rotates.
An imaginary vertical plane that divides the body into left and right halves; movements in this plane involve forward or backward motion.
A horizontal axis running from side to side through the body, around which forward and backward rotations occur; matches the sagittal plane.
An imaginary vertical plane that divides the body into front and back halves; movements in this plane involve side-to-side motion such as abduction and adduction.
A horizontal axis running from front to back through the body, around which side-to-side rotations occur; matches the frontal plane. OCR's term for this axis.
An imaginary horizontal plane that divides the body into upper and lower halves; movements in this plane involve twisting or spinning.
A vertical axis running from the top of the head to the feet, around which twisting and spinning rotations occur; matches the transverse plane.

hero_image_caption: Planes and axes of movement describe the direction and rotation of the body in sport.
narration_script: When a gymnast performs a forward somersault or a discus thrower spins in a full circle, we can describe those movements precisely using planes and axes. Imagine three flat surfaces slicing through the body at right angles to each other. These are the three planes of movement, each with a matching axis. The sagittal plane divides the body into left and right halves. Movement here is forwards or backwards. The matching axis is the transverse axis, which runs side to side through the hips. A forward somersault uses the sagittal plane and transverse axis. The frontal plane divides the body into front and back halves. Movement here is side to side. The matching axis in OCR is the frontal axis, which runs front to back through the body. A cartwheel uses the frontal plane and frontal axis. The transverse plane divides the body into upper and lower halves. Movement here is twisting or spinning. The matching axis is the longitudinal axis, which runs vertically from head to feet. A 360 degree ice spin uses the transverse plane and longitudinal axis. An important OCR-specific point: OCR calls the axis of the frontal plane the frontal axis. Some other boards use the term sagittal axis for the same axis, but that term is not used in OCR. Always write frontal axis for movements in the frontal plane.
